analysis.one_liner: Limits commercials in children's TV shows and makes stations answer for kids' programming at license renewal.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee after hearings, and never got a floor vote; Congress later enacted a similar children's TV advertising limit in 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill ordered the FCC to write rules capping commercials in children's TV programs at no more than 10.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes per hour on weekdays. It also told the FCC to weigh a broadcaster's compliance with those limits, and its service to children's educational needs, when deciding whether to renew the station's broadcast license. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Children watching commercial television, and parents concerned about advertising aimed at kids. The caps would reduce the number of commercials per hour in children's programming, and license-renewal scrutiny would pressure stations to air educational content for children.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and parents watching broadcast TV

how_it_helps.text: Caps advertising during children's programs at no more than 10.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes per hour on weekdays, starting January 1, 1990.
Requires the FCC to start writing those rules within 30 days and finish within 150 days of enactment, giving the agency hard deadlines instead of discretion to delay.

Requires the FCC, when deciding whether to renew a station's broadcast license, to consider both compliance with the ad limits and whether the station has served children's educational and informational needs.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial broadcasters, who would sell fewer advertising minutes in children's programs, and the advertisers that buy those minutes, especially toy and food marketers aimed at kids.

drawbacks.text: The bill still relied on advertiser financing of children's programs, affirming in its findings that 'the financial support of advertisers assists in the provision of programming to children' rather than funding children's programming through any public means.

The advertising limits allowed the FCC to modify or weaken them after January 1, 1993 following notice, public comment, and a public-interest demonstration, so the caps were not permanently locked in.

The programming provision only required the FCC to 'consider' a station's children's educational programming at license renewal, leaving the FCC discretion and no explicit mandate for a minimum amount of educational programming.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill imposed a modest, well-defined cost — fewer ad minutes per hour in children's programming — on broadcasters in exchange for hard deadlines and enforceable limits that the FCC's then-voluntary approach lacked. It was not aimed at industry payback: it still allowed advertiser support of children's programming and even let the FCC relax the standards after 1993 if the public interest justified it. The main design weakness is that its programming provision relies on the FCC considering children's service at renewal rather than prescribing educational quotas. On balance a low-cost, targeted consumer-protection measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 5, 1989 and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On July 12, 1989, the Communications Subcommittee held the only recorded congressional action on the bill: hearings (S.Hrg. 101-221).
After the July 1989 hearing, the record shows no markup, no committee report, and no floor action through the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadcasters and advertisers kept unrestricted commercial minutes in children's programming for the life of the 101st Congress; a companion version of the restriction was enacted in the Children's Television Act of 1990.

for.name: Howard M. Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate children's TV advertising limits and enforce broadcasters' educational obligations.

for.name: Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: Senate Communications Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill on July 12, 1989 (S.Hrg. 101-221).

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in April 1989 and never reported it out; after the July 1989 subcommittee hearing, no markup or committee vote appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only one cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no roll-call record shows how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill capped ad minutes in children's programming at 10.5 minutes per hour weekends and 12 on weekdays, cutting ad inventory, and exposed stations to FCC scrutiny of their children's programming at license renewal.

industries.industry: Advertisers and children's toy and product marketers
industries.note: Fewer commercial minutes per hour in children's blocks meant less advertising time to sell to companies marketing to kids, one of the advertising industry's most lucrative audiences.
